The idea of dropout is that at training time, every time you are doing a piece of training with an example, what you're going to do is, inside the middle layers of the neural network, you're just going to throw away some of the inputs. And technically the way you do this is you have a random mask that you sample each time of zeros and ones; you do a Hadamard product of that with the data, so some of the data items go to zero. And you have a different

**[14:48]** mask each time, so for the next thing you know I've now masked out something different this time. So you're just randomly throwing away the inputs. And the effect of this is that you're training the model so that it has to be robust and work well and make as much use of every input as it can. It can't decide that it can be extremely reliant on, you know, component 17 of the vector, because sometimes it's just going to randomly disappear. So if there are other features that you could use instead that would let you work out what to do next, you should also know how to make use of those features. So at

**[15:33]** training time you randomly delete things; at test time, sort of for efficiency but also quality of the answer, you don't delete anything, you keep all of your weights, but you just rescale things to make up for the fact that you used to be dropping things. Okay. There are several ways that you can think of explaining this. One motivation that's often given is that this prevents feature co-adaptation: so rather than a model being able to learn complex functions of "feature 7, 8 and 11 can help me predict this", it knows that some of the features might be missing, so it has to make use of things in a more flexible

**[16:18]** way. Another way of thinking of it is that there's been a lot of work on model ensembles, where you can mix together different models and improve your results. If you're training with dropout, it's kind of like you're training with a huge model ensemble, because you're training with the ensemble of the power set — the exponential number of every possible dropout of features — all at once, and that gives you a very good model. So there are different ways of thinking about it. If you've seen naïve Bayes and logistic regression models before, I kind of think a nice way to think of it is that it gives a sort of middle ground between the two, because for naïve Bayes models you're weighting

**[17:04]** each feature independently just based on the data statistics, doesn't matter what other features are there; in a logistic regression, weights are set in the context of all the other features; and with dropout you're somewhere in between — you're seeing the weights in the context of some of the other features, but different ones will disappear at different times. Following work that was done at Stanford by Stefan Wager and others, generally these days people regard dropout as a form of feature-dependent regularization, and he shows some theoretical results as to why to think of it that way. **[35:41]** that people just hacked the counts a little to make it non-zero. So there are lots of ways that are explored, but the easiest way is you just add a little delta, like 0.25, to counts. **[36:26]** standard trick that was used then was that you did backoff. **[52:42]** probabilities for the next word, we're going to do something different. So our hidden layer is going to be *recurrent*, and by recurrent it means we're going to change a hidden state at each time step as we proceed through the text from left to right. So we're going to start off with an **h**⁰, which is the initial hidden state, which can actually just be all zeros. And then at each time step, what we're going to do is we're going to multiply the previous hidden state by a weight matrix, we're going to take a word embedding and multiply it by a weight matrix, and then we're going to sum the results

**[53:28]** of those two things, and that's going to give us a new hidden state. So that hidden state will then store a memory of everything that's been seen so far. So we'll do that and then we'll continue along, so we'll multiply the next word vector by the same weight matrix, we multiply the previous hidden state by the same weight matrix **W**_h each time, and we add them together and get a new representation. You're adding on a bias term, because we usually separate out a bias term, and you're putting things through a

**[54:14]** nonlinearity. So I should make sure I mention that. And for recurrent neural networks, most commonly this nonlinearity has actually been the tanh function, so it's balanced on the positive-negative side. And so you keep on doing that through each step. And so the idea is, once we've got to here, this **h**⁴ hidden state is a hidden state that in some sense has read the text up until now — it's seen all of "the students opened their". And if the word "students" occurred in any of these positions, it will have been multiplied by the same weight matrix and added into the hidden state. So it's got a cleaner, low-parameter way of incorporating in

**[54:59]** the information that's seen. Well, the softmax will give me a language model of probability over all next words, and I can sample from it to generate the next word. Does that make sense? Okay. Recurrent neural networks.

**[55:48]** Okay, so with recurrent neural networks we can now process any length of preceding context, and we'll just put more and more stuff in our hidden state. Our computation is using information from many steps back. Our model size doesn't increase for having a long context — we have to do more computation for a long context, but our representation of that long context just remains this fixed-size hidden vector **h** of whatever dimension it is, so there's no exponential blowout anymore. There's the same weights applied at every time step, so there's a

**[56:33]** symmetry in how inputs are processed. There are some catches. The biggest catch in practice is that recurrent computation is slow. So for the feed-forward layer we just had our input vector, we multiply it by a matrix, we multiply it by a matrix however many times, and then at the end we're done. Whereas here we're stuck with this sequentiality, that you have to be doing one hidden vector at a time. And that's one of the big problems with RNNs that have

**[57:21]** led them to fall out of favor. There's another problem that we'll look at more, which is that in theory this is perfect — you're just incorporating all of the past context in your hidden vector. In practice it tends not to work perfectly, because although stuff you saw back here is in some sense still alive in the hidden vector as you come across here, your memory of it gets more and more distant, and it's the words that you saw recently that dominate the hidden state. Now in some sense that's right, because the recent stuff is the most important stuff that's freshest in your mind — it's the same with human beings, they

**[58:08]** tend to forget stuff from further back as well. So for training an RNN language model, the starting-off point is we get a big corpus of text again, and then we're going to compute for each time step a prediction of the probability of next words, and then there's going to be an actual next word, and we're going to use that as

**[58:54]** the basis of our loss. So our loss function is the cross-entropy between the predicted probability and what the actual next word that we saw is — which again, as in the example I showed before, is just the negative log likelihood of the actual next word. Ideally you'd like to predict the actual next word with probability one, which means the negative log of one would be zero and there'd be no loss; but in practice, if you give it an estimate of 0.5 there's only a little bit of loss, and so on. And so to get our overall objective function, we work out the average loss, the average

**[59:39]** negative log likelihood of predicting each word in turn. Okay, there's a loss for that, the negative log prob given to "students". We then go on and generate the probability estimate over the next words, and then we say, well,

**[1:00:26]** the actual word is "opened", what probability estimate did you give to that? We get a negative log-probability loss. Keep on running this along, and then we sum all of those losses and we average them per word, and that's our average per-word loss, and we want to make that as small as possible. And so that's our training mechanism. And it's important to note that for generating this loss we're not just doing free generation. We're not just saying to the model, go off and generate a sentence. What we're actually doing is, at each step we're effectively saying, okay, the prefix is "the students opened",

**[1:01:13]** what probability distribution do you put on next words after that? And then again we use the actual next word. So we do one step of generation, then we pull it back to what was actually in the text, and then

**[1:01:59]** we ask it for guesses over the next word, and repeat forever.
